stem: Which broader change in federal Indian policy does Joseph's surrender best illustrate?

stimulus.source_note: Chief Joseph's surrender message, Bear Paw Mountains, Montana Territory, October 1877, as transcribed by Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood, aide to General Howard; printed in Harper's Weekly, November 17, 1877. Public domain. Text verified against the University of Washington Libraries transcription of Harper's Weekly and the National Park Service account of the Nez Perce surrender.
stimulus.text:
Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, surrender message, Bear Paw Mountains, Montana Territory, October 1877 (as transcribed by Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood; ellipses mark omissions):

"Tell General Howard I know his heart. What he told me before I have in my heart. I am tired of fighting. Our chiefs are killed. Looking Glass is dead. Tu-hul-hul-sote is dead. The old men are all dead. It is the young men who say yes or no. He who led the young men is dead. It is cold and we have no blankets. The little children are freezing to death. My people, some of them, have run away to the hills, and have no blankets, no food. No one knows where they are - perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children, and see how many of them I can find. Maybe I shall find them among the dead. Hear me, my chiefs. I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever."

options.text: The shift from treating tribes as nations to forcing them onto reservations
The shift from allotment back to large tribal reservations
options.misconception: Background: allotment came later, with the Dawes Act of 1887; in 1877 the government was still forcing tribes onto reservations.

options.text: The shift from military force to negotiated purchases of tribal land
options.misconception: Background: the army pursued the Nez Perce for months; this surrender followed force, not a purchase.

options.text: The shift from reservations to full tribal independence
options.misconception: Background: Joseph surrendered because independence had been lost, not because it had been granted.

rationales.A: Joseph is not negotiating a treaty; he is surrendering to the army after being ordered onto a reservation. Background: the old treaty system was giving way to forced removal and army control.
rationales.B: Background: allotment came later, with the Dawes Act of 1887. In 1877 the government was still forcing tribes onto reservations.
rationales.C: Background: the army pursued the Nez Perce for months. This surrender followed force, not a purchase.
rationales.D: Background: Joseph surrendered because independence had been lost, not because it had been granted.
rationales.general:
Picture a chief who once negotiated as the head of a nation, now handing over his rifle to a colonel.
1. Ask what Joseph is doing. He is surrendering, not signing a treaty between equals.
2. Ask what order put him here. Background: The government ordered his band onto a small Idaho reservation and sent the army when they resisted.
3. Name the change. Background: Tribes were no longer treated as nations to bargain with; they were peoples to be moved and managed.
Remember: when a treaty partner becomes a prisoner, the policy has changed even if the words stay polite.
